narrative:
Based on the assessment, there is a 17% chance you will fail your final year. While this may seem relatively low, it exceeds the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for remedial courses, meaning additional academic support has been deemed necessary for you.

The three factors that most shaped this prediction all actually worked in your favor, reducing your likelihood of failing — yet not enough to bring the risk below the required threshold.

The most influential factor was your clean academic record: you have no history of past failures, which strongly suggests you are capable of meeting academic expectations. This was the single biggest reason the model did not predict a higher risk of failure.

The second most important factor was your ambition to pursue higher education. Your aspiration to continue studying beyond school signals motivation and a forward-looking mindset, which the model recognized as a protective factor.

Third, your father's higher education level also contributed positively. Compared to other students not required to take remedial courses, where nearly half have fathers with only a 5th-to-9th grade education, your father's higher qualification suggests a more academically supportive home environment.

Despite these positive signals, other aspects of your profile — such as studying less than two hours per week, which is notably lower than the two-to-five hour range typical among students not in remedial courses, and spending a high amount of time going out with friends — likely kept your overall risk elevated.

You are encouraged to increase your weekly study time and take full advantage of the remedial courses to secure a successful outcome this year.
